title: Owl on a branch in cross-stitch
subtitle: A tawny owl perched on a bare branch, on 14-count Aida
excerpt: An owl on a branch is a 65-by-80 stitch piece worked on 14-count Aida in warm browns, cream, and amber. The round face disc and feather barring are the two key shapes to establish from the centre outward. The finished piece is about 12 x 14 cm in a 15 cm hoop.
sourceNotes: Original design for Homemade cross-stitch library. Owl motifs appear widely in needlework traditions; this design follows natural history illustration colouring conventions.

content.text: An owl on a branch is a 65-by-80 stitch piece on 14-count
. The palette is warm browns, cream, and amber, nine
colours in total. The distinctive circular face disc and the horizontal feather barring on the breast are the two shapes that give an owl its character. Both are built entirely from
; the back-stitch layer adds the talon detail and the eye ring at the end.

items.name: 14-count Aida, cream or natural
items.substitutions: Pale grey Aida gives the creamy plumage more contrast

content.text: Find the fabric centre and mount in the hoop. The chart centre falls in the face disc. Begin there with the pale cream (3866) that fills the face and work outward.

Work the face disc in pale colours first, then add the darker shading around the outer ring of the disc (3033, 3782). Next work the upper body and wing pattern in the mid and dark browns (3790, 610, 938).
Stitch the branch in dark brown (938, 3371) with long horizontal rows. The talon grip is two short vertical lines on each foot in 3371.
Add the amber eyes (3820, single stitch each) last, then surround each with a one-stitch back-stitch ring in 3371. The back-stitch detail turns two coloured squares into recognisable owl eyes.
Wash gently and press face-down until the stitches sit smooth and flat. Display in the hoop or trim and frame under glass. The brown palette suits a dark-stained wooden frame or an olive-green mount.

items.symptom: The face disc looks square rather than circular
items.cause: The outer row of the disc was stitched as a straight edge instead of following the stepped curve on the chart.
items.fix: Count the stepping carefully on the chart: the disc edge has single-stitch steps at the corners. Work those single stitches first, then fill inward. Once all the outer stepping is in, the circular shape should read clearly.

items.symptom: The branch looks smudged at the join to the talon
items.cause: The talon detail back-stitch was worked before the surrounding cross-stitches were complete, and later stitches covered part of it.
items.fix: Always add back-stitch detail last, when all cross-stitches in the area are finished. Work the talon lines once the surrounding branch colour is complete and stable.

content.text: The same approach works for any perching bird. A robin on a holly branch uses a very similar composition with a different palette.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads. The default for beginners. Counted in squares per inch: 11ct, 14ct, 16ct, and 18ct are the common counts.

The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch. Each skein is made of six strands twisted together loosely; the stitcher strips out the number of strands needed for the fabric count (two strands for 14-count Aida) and threads them together.
